raw_comment: Researchers from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention have collected data on the consumption of tobacco products by middle school and high school students from 2011-2018. This information is displayed in the graph to the left, and there are two distinct lines per age group, one regarding tobacco products at large, and the other specifically concerning e-cigarettes. I notice that while the use of any tobacco products has increased for middle schoolers in 2017 from roughly 4% to 7% of students, the use of any tobacco products for high schoolers has significantly jumped in 2017 from about 19% to about 27% of students. I see that the line describing the use of exclusively e-cigarettes is identical to the upward trend of the line depicting the use of any tobacco product, which makes me thinks that e-cigarettes are the major contributor to the growth in consumption over the past seven years. Perhaps this is the obvious question, but I wonder why this is? I have a hard time coming to any solid answer to this question. Also, what could the government do to deter the continuation of this pattern? A month ago, I heard in the news that the FDA is working on banning popular flavors of pods for Juuls, a very popular e-cigarette brand, that students might find appealing, such as mango and mint. How else could the government aid this situation? Is the federal government’s intervention constitutional?

raw_comment: Vaping: One of the most prominent epidemics among teenagers. I was almost waiting for a graph about it to appear on this site. This graph calculates the percentage of students in both middle school and high school that have used any tobacco product versus e-cigarettes. My eye is immediately drawn to the E-cigarette uprising. The number of high school students using e-cigarettes, or "juuls", has increased from about 2% to about 21% from 2011-2018. Additionally, the middle school percantage of e-cigarette users has increased by about 5%. This statistic does NOT surprise me. I've seen so many teenagers around me vaping, and it's sad as they soon become addicted to nicotine. Teenagers don't realize that though they may look "cool" or impress their peers, they are placing themselves on a dangerous path. Other tobacco products have been on a steady pace for middle schoolers at around 8%. High schoolers, on the other hand, appear to have stopped using Tobacco products between 2016-2017. However, they are now on the rise again with about 27% of students using them. Though we are unsure of the health risks that new tobacco technology entails, we know that it is not good for us. However, the companies that sell them are certainly having a good time.
